blocks.text: Vertebrates have a vertebral column and a cranium. They are divided into seven classes, placed in two groups. Group Pisces includes three classes, Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes; these are fishes and have no limbs. Group Tetrapoda includes four classes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia; these have four limbs.

blocks.alt: A chart. Vertebrates split into two groups. Pisces (no limbs) holds three classes: Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes. Tetrapoda (four limbs) holds four classes: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.
blocks.caption: The seven classes of vertebrates in their two groups (original chart).
blocks.long_description: Fishes make up group Pisces: jawless fishes, cartilaginous fishes and bony fishes. The four-limbed classes make up group Tetrapoda: amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

blocks.text: Group Pisces
1. Class Cyclostomata

These are the jawless fishes; lampreys and hagfish are common examples. The body is eel-like and not covered with scales. The skeleton is cartilaginous. Like other fishes they have a single-circuit heart, with one atrium and one ventricle. Fertilisation is external.
2. Class Chondrichthyes

This class includes sharks, skates, rays and ratfishes. The skeleton is made of cartilage. The body is covered by placoid (tooth-like) scales called denticles. They have jaws and biting mouthparts. The pectoral and pelvic fins are paired, and there are two dorsal fins. The heart is single-circuit, with one atrium and one ventricle. Behind each eye is a small opening called a spiracle, used for breathing. They have no swim bladder. Fertilisation is internal.
3. Class Osteichthyes

The bony fishes have a bony endoskeleton, a streamlined body, dermal bony scales and a terminal mouth with jaws, with or without teeth. The notochord is replaced by the vertebral column, although some bony fishes keep it in a reduced form. A swim bladder helps with buoyancy. They have both median fins (dorsal, caudal and ventral) and paired fins (pelvic and pectoral). There are four pairs of gills, protected by a bony flap, the operculum. The nervous system is well developed, with ten pairs of cranial nerves. Fertilisation is mostly external. Freshwater bony fishes include rohu, trout, katla and catfish; marine bony fishes include the seahorse, the flying fish and the angler fish.

blocks.alt: A side view of a bony fish with its fins and organs labelled: dorsal fin on the back, caudal fin at the tail, pectoral and pelvic fins in pairs on the sides and underside, the operculum covering the gills behind the head, and inside the body the swim bladder above the stomach and intestine.
blocks.caption: External features of a bony fish (original diagram after Figure 1.22).
blocks.long_description: The median fins are the dorsal fin, the caudal (tail) fin and the ventral fin. The paired fins are the pectoral and pelvic fins. The operculum is the bony flap over the gills. The swim bladder lies inside the body cavity and gives buoyancy.

blocks.text: Group Tetrapoda
4. Class Amphibia

Amphibia is the first class of tetrapods. They have a bony endoskeleton. Unlike fishes, amphibians have a neck: the first (cervical) vertebra moves against the back of the skull and lets the skull nod vertically. The skin is smooth, without scales, and moist. It helps in gas exchange, temperature regulation and the absorption and storage of water. The heart is double-circuit and three-chambered, with two atria and one ventricle. They breathe with gills in the larval stage and with lungs and skin as adults.

Amphibians depend on an external heat source, so they are ectotherms. They cannot regulate their body temperature or keep it constant, so they are poikilothermic, and they hibernate in winter. Salamanders, newts and mud puppies are tailed amphibians; frogs and toads are tail-less; caecilians are legless. Amphibians are unisexual, and fertilisation is usually external.
5. Class Reptilia

Reptiles are the first animal group with amniotic eggs. An amniotic egg makes protective extra-embryonic membranes, the amnion, allantois and chorion, which protect the embryo from drying out, nourish it and let it develop on land. The egg contains a large amount of yolk, the embryo's main food supply, and abundant albumin, which provides extra nutrients and water. It is covered by a leathery, calcareous shell that is partly permeable to gases but not to water.

Reptiles have dry, scaly skin. The bony endoskeleton is harder than that of amphibians, and the skull is longer. The first two cervical vertebrae, the atlas and the axis, allow more movement of the head. In the heart the ventricle is incompletely partitioned into left and right ventricles. Like amphibians, reptiles are ectothermic and use an external heat source for thermoregulation; they cannot keep a constant body temperature and are poikilotherms. Fertilisation is internal, and they are oviparous (egg-laying). Present-day reptiles are the lizards, snakes, tuatara and crocodiles.
6. Class Aves

Birds have a covering of feathers. Feathers form the flight surfaces that provide lift and help steering, and they also prevent heat and water loss. Birds are endotherms: they obtain heat from cellular processes, and this internal heat source lets them maintain a nearly constant core temperature. Animals that keep their core temperature constant are homeotherms.

The body is streamlined and spindle-shaped. The forelimbs are modified into wings. The bones are light because of large air spaces. A lighter sheath called the bill replaces the teeth. The sternum (chest bone) bears a large bone, the keel, for the attachment of the flight muscles. Bills and tongues are modified for many feeding habits and food sources.

In many birds a diverticulum of the oesophagus called the crop stores food so that a bird can quickly take in a large amount. A region of the stomach called the gizzard has muscular walls that crush food. The heart is four-chambered, with complete separation of the atria and ventricles. The nervous system is highly developed, and vision and hearing are the most important senses for most birds. The external nares open into the pharynx through the nasal passages; the pharynx leads to the trachea and then the bronchi. The organ of voice, the syrinx, sits at the lower end of the trachea. The bronchi lead into a complex system of air sacs that occupy much of the body and even extend into some bones. The air sacs connect to lungs made of small air tubes called parabronchi.

Like reptiles and mammals, birds have amniotic eggs with large amounts of yolk and albumin, covered by a leathery shell. Fertilisation is internal and development is external: birds are oviparous. Some birds have secondarily lost the power of flight and are called running birds, for example the ostrich, kiwi, rhea, cassowary and emu. Flying birds include the pigeon, parrot, crow, eagle and robin.
7. Class Mammalia

Mammals are vertebrates nourished by milk from the mammary glands of the mother, and they have hair on the body. The skin has glands developed from the epidermis: sebaceous (oil) glands secrete an oily secretion, and sudoriferous (sweat) glands release watery secretions used in evaporative cooling. Mammary glands are functional in females. Most mammals have two sets of teeth during their lives, milk teeth and permanent teeth. An external ear, the pinna, is present, and the middle ear has a chain of three bones: incus, malleus and stapes.

Mammals are endothermic and homeothermic. They have a four-chambered heart and a muscular diaphragm that separates the coelom into thoracic and abdominal cavities. The voice apparatus is well developed: a larynx with vocal cords, and an epiglottis. Fertilisation is internal. Most mammals, the placental mammals, give birth to young and are viviparous; some lay eggs and are oviparous; and some are marsupials. There are three groups.

items: Egg-laying mammals lay eggs in which the whole development of the embryo takes place. They are found in Australia: the duckbill platypus and the echidna (spiny anteater).

Marsupials have a pouch, the marsupium, on the abdomen of the female. They give birth to immature young, which complete their development in the mother's pouch; they are called ovoviviparous. Examples are the opossum, the kangaroo and the Tasmanian wolf.

Placental mammals are the most advanced mammals. During development a structure called the placenta forms between the wall of the mother's uterus and the body of the foetus. The foetus is nourished, and its wastes are removed, through the placenta. Examples are the dolphin, rat, monkey, bat, elephant and human.
